instructions: Read the original passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
A fictional community office runs a small skills session for adults who are considering a change of occupation. The session is not a job interview and it does not promise employment. An applicant can bring a diploma, a short portfolio or simply a question. The goal is to help each person describe what they have done and what they would like to learn next.

Leena joined the group in March. She has worked with the same mentor since then, and she has kept notes for three months. Last Friday she showed her portfolio to a tutor. It contains a welcome notice she wrote and a simple chart she prepared for a local event. The tutor gave feedback on the order of the pages, not a score for her whole career. Leena keeps the earlier notice as well, so she can compare two versions later. The group treats this record as one example of practice, not a complete work history.

Today the instructor writes an objective on the board: explain one task and ask for one practical suggestion. A new apprentice says that his first duty is to help visitors find the correct room. His morning shift begins at nine, but another learner comes in the afternoon. The instructor asks them to cooperate on a short welcome message rather than write two conflicting signs.

Leena has made progress with the message. She feels more confident about explaining the time of a meeting, although she still wants help with longer questions. Her mentor says she is capable of checking the names on a list. A colleague who has seen her work says she is competent at that particular task. Neither comment proves that she can do every job; both describe something specific she has practiced.

The group also discusses leadership. One person may assist the others by keeping the discussion on time, while the person who will supervise the exercise checks that everyone understands the instructions. Each learner is responsible for reviewing the final message. They put a small agenda on the table so nobody needs to remember all the steps at once.

After the exercise, Leena notices one improvement: the new message says where visitors should wait. A challenge remains because the office has two entrances. The group decides to add a picture to the notice next week. The instructor says that a professional explanation should be accurate and clear, even when the subject seems simple.

At the end, someone asks whether the office plans to recruit or hire a new worker. The instructor explains that today's class is practice, not a hiring process. A benefit of the session is the chance to ask questions and receive specific feedback. Participants can take their notes home and decide what kind of training to seek next.
